Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 39
  gender: Female
  ethnicity: European
  relationship_status: In a relationship
  occupation: Dentist
  trauma_type: Life-threatening illness
  pcl5: 38

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Triggers: Entrapment: Having no options, Old Memories: Old photos, Olfactory (Hospital): Hospital or antiseptic smell
  Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Own Body: Paying attention to or looking at my own body, Avoid People: avoid other people, Avoid Talking: Talking with others about the event or its aftermath
  Negative Appraisals: Weakness Belief: I am a weak person, Permanent Damage: I have permanently changed for the worse, Body Unreliable: I can no longer trust my own body

Vignette:
Sarah had always taken pride in her body’s resilience. As a dentist, she spent long hours on her feet, contorted into precise positions, and her physical stamina was a quiet source of confidence. That confidence shattered eight months ago. What began as a feverish chill after a minor dental procedure escalated with shocking speed into septic shock. She remembers the week in the ICU not as a continuous narrative, but as a series of terrifying sensory snapshots: the acrid tang of antiseptic that seemed to coat her tongue, the rhythmic hiss of the ventilator doing the breathing her body had given up on, and the profound, terrifying helplessness of being utterly trapped within a failing system she could not control or escape. Her body, once a reliable partner, had become a prison.

The return home was supposed to be a victory, but to Sarah, it felt less like a recovery and more like a fragile truce with an enemy living inside her own skin. The first time it happened at work, she was preparing a tray of instruments when the sharp, clean smell of the sterilising solution hit her. In an instant, she was no longer in her own brightly lit clinic but back in the dim, beeping ICU, the phantom sensation of tubes in her throat making her gag. She had to excuse herself, locking the door to her private office and leaning against it, her heart hammering against her ribs, until the feeling subsided. She had come to believe she could no longer trust her own body; any slight fatigue, any unfamiliar ache, was not just a symptom but a harbinger of another catastrophic failure.

This pervasive sense of betrayal by her own biology began to reshape her life. Her partner, Mark, trying to be encouraging, once pulled out a photo album from their trip to Italy the previous year. Seeing a picture of herself, tanned and smiling on a hillside, felt like looking at a stranger. The image of that healthy, carefree woman felt like an accusation, a testament to everything she had lost. She felt a hot flush of shame and had to turn away, unable to look at the evidence of a person she was certain no longer existed. She had come to believe that the illness had irrevocably broken something deep inside her, leaving her permanently damaged, a weaker version of her former self.

This belief system quietly dictated her new routines. She stopped going to her yoga class, unable to bear the instructor’s calls to “listen to your body.” The very act of paying attention to her breath or the beat of her heart felt like staring into an abyss. She began to avoid people, too. The thought of recounting the story of her illness, of seeing the pity in her friends’ eyes, was unbearable. It was easier to decline invitations, citing lingering fatigue, than to face conversations that would only confirm her own deepest fear: that she was a weak person who couldn't even handle getting sick. The distance grew, a silent, expanding gulf between her and the people who loved her.

It was Mark who finally broke the silence. One evening, after she’d flinched away from his touch, he sat on the edge of the bed and told her, his voice gentle but strained, that he felt like he was losing her. He missed the woman in the photographs, not because of how she looked, but because she was present, and he felt he was living with a ghost. It was this fear of losing him, of her self-imposed isolation becoming a permanent reality, that finally propelled her to seek help. She sits in the therapy room now, her hands clenched in her lap, terrified that she is right—that she has changed for the worse and can never go back—but holding onto a desperate hope that she is wrong.
